title: The Workers Who Built the Pyramids
text:
For centuries people imagined the Great Pyramid being raised by vast gangs of slaves under the whip. Herodotus, writing two thousand years after it was built, said a hundred thousand men worked in shifts of three months. Excavations at Giza since the late twentieth century have given a different picture.

From 1990 the Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass excavated a cemetery of the pyramid builders on the slope south of the monuments. The workers had been buried with honor near the kings they served, with bread and beer for the afterlife, and some tombs carried the titles of gang supervisors and skilled craftsmen. Skeletons showed the strain of heavy labor, but also healed fractures and evidence of medical care.

Nearby, a team led by the American archaeologist Mark Lehner uncovered a large settlement often called the Lost City of the Pyramid Builders: bakeries, breweries, storerooms and long galleries that probably housed rotating crews. Animal bones showed that the workers were fed large amounts of meat, including beef.

Inscriptions and graffiti suggest how the labor was organized. Crews had names, such as Friends of Khufu or Drunkards of Menkaure, and were divided into smaller groups that competed and worked in rotation. A permanent core of skilled craftsmen was joined by larger numbers of laborers drawn from villages across Egypt for periods of service. They were not free volunteers in the modern sense, but neither were they slaves.
lesson: Great works are built by organized teams with names, pride and care for each other. Treat people as members of a crew, not as tools.
people: Mark Lehner, Zahi Hawass, pyramid builders of Giza
source: Mark Lehner, The Complete Pyramids (1997); Zahi Hawass and Mark Lehner, excavation reports of the Giza Plateau Mapping Project and the workers' cemetery
caveat: Labor was probably rotating compulsory service owed to the state, so the line between paid work and obligation remains debated.
